skill.name: write-contract
skill.description: Guidance for writing production GenLayer intelligent contracts with pinned runner dependencies, explicit consensus rules, safe storage patterns, LLM resilience, and cross-contract interaction.
skill.summary: Guides production GenLayer contract design with pinned runners, validator logic, storage rules, and resilient LLM handling.
skill.author: internet-court

security_audit.summary: The audit confirmed the eval guidance in SKILL.md lines 393-412 as a real dynamic code execution risk because it recommends evaluating LLM-generated Python expressions. The cross-chain RPC example also introduces low-risk outbound network access. The remaining backtick, key, and reconnaissance detections are Markdown or terminology false positives, and no prompt injection attempt was found.

remediation.issue: LLM-generated expressions are evaluated with eval().
remediation.suggestion: Replace the eval pattern with a small parser, declarative rule schema, or approved predicate library. Keep generated code out of contract execution paths.

remediation.issue: Network RPC examples accept arbitrary rpc_url values.
remediation.suggestion: Use allowlisted RPC endpoints or validate domains before web requests. Document that user-supplied URLs can create network abuse risk.

content.value_statement: GenLayer contracts need pinned runners, stable consensus rules, and careful LLM handling. This skill guides Claude, Codex, and Claude Code through production contract design and review.
actual_capabilities: Creates GenLayer contract skeletons with pinned GenVM runner dependency headers.
Guides selection of strict equality, comparative prompts, or custom validator functions.
Explains storage declarations using GenLayer types such as TreeMap, DynArray, u256, and i256.
Provides patterns for parsing LLM output and classifying expected, external, transient, and LLM errors.
Covers cross-contract reads, emitted writes, factory deployment, and cross-chain RPC verification.
Recommends linting, direct mode tests, and integration tests before deployment.
limitations: It is guidance only; users must still test contracts in their own GenLayer environment.
Examples may need adaptation for current GenLayer SDK APIs and network rules.
It cannot guarantee legal, economic, or consensus safety for deployed contracts.
The eval-based example requires careful security review before production use.

use_cases.title: Build a Dispute Contract
use_cases.description: Product teams can convert escrow or appeal rules into a contract design with evidence, settlement, and validator boundaries.

use_cases.title: Review Consensus Logic
use_cases.description: Smart contract developers can choose the right equivalence principle and avoid leader-only validation for AI or web outputs.

use_cases.title: Harden Contract Storage
use_cases.description: Protocol engineers can apply storage, error, and upgrade rules before deploying contracts that manage persistent state.

prompt_templates.title: Draft a Basic Contract
prompt_templates.prompt: Use write-contract to draft a GenLayer contract for my feature. Include the pinned runner, storage fields, public methods, and tests.

prompt_templates.title: Choose Consensus Boundaries
prompt_templates.prompt: Use write-contract to decide what belongs on-chain for this workflow: [describe workflow]. Identify evidence, settlement effects, and off-chain duties.

prompt_templates.title: Harden LLM Validation
prompt_templates.prompt: Use write-contract to review this LLM-based contract flow. Improve the equivalence principle, validator checks, error handling, and parsing strategy.

prompt_templates.title: Design Cross-Contract Workflow
prompt_templates.prompt: Use write-contract to design a multi-contract GenLayer workflow with emitted writes, worker deployment, RPC verification, storage layout, and integration tests.

output_examples.input: Create a GenLayer contract for moderation appeals with submitted evidence.
output_examples.output: A contract outline with pinned runner guidance, appeal records, submit and resolve methods, comparative validation criteria, and required tests.

output_examples.input: Review my idea for settling a prediction from a public website.
output_examples.output: A boundary note that keeps previews off-chain, fetches source evidence during settlement, derives stable status, and avoids variable fields.

output_examples.input: Improve LLM parsing for a scoring contract.
output_examples.output: A parsing plan with response format guidance, key aliases, numeric coercion, typed error prefixes, and validator agreement rules.

best_practices: Pin the GenVM runner version before writing contract logic.
Make validators independently verify the leader result against source data or a second run.
Run linting and consensus integration tests before deployment.
anti_patterns: Using py-genlayer:test, py-genlayer:latest, or unversioned runner aliases in generated contracts.
Checking only response shape or labels while accepting the leader's substantive answer.
Storing Python lists, dictionaries, floats for money, or enums directly in contract state.

faq.question: What does this skill help create?
faq.answer: It helps create GenLayer intelligent contracts with pinned runners, validator logic, storage rules, and test guidance.

faq.question: Does it write deployment-ready contracts?
faq.answer: It provides production-focused guidance, but users must lint, test, and review every contract before deployment.

faq.question: Which tools can use it?
faq.answer: The report lists support for Claude, Codex, and Claude Code.

faq.question: Does it handle LLM outputs?
faq.answer: Yes. It recommends response formatting, defensive parsing, error classification, and validator comparison rules.

faq.question: Can it design cross-contract flows?
faq.answer: Yes. It covers contract reads, emitted writes, factory deployment, and RPC verification patterns.

faq.question: What should users review carefully?
faq.answer: Users should review consensus rules, external network calls, storage layout, and any eval-based generated code pattern.
